The first time I realized how loud silence could be was late afternoon, when the street outside my window had finally gone quiet. Not empty-quiet, not bedtime quiet, but that in-between hush when the day seems to hold its breath. A bus groaned somewhere far off, and then even that sound softened into distance, leaving the room with its own small noises: the tick of a clock, the faint click of radiator metal cooling, the soft breath of whatever I was doing when I thought nobody was listening.

I used to believe silence was a lack—an absence you filled with music, conversation, or noise. But that evening it felt more like presence. It sat in the corners without demanding attention, like a book left open on a table. If I stayed still long enough, I could almost hear the thoughts I normally hurried past. They weren’t dramatic. They were ordinary: worry about a message I hadn’t sent, a memory of a joke someone laughed at, the sudden tenderness of remembering someone’s name.

Silence didn’t solve anything, but it changed the shape of my day. It made everything less urgent. It allowed me to notice that I was tired, that I was trying, that I had been carrying more than I admitted. When I finally stood up and turned on a lamp, the light didn’t defeat the quiet. It just joined it.

I think that’s what some kinds of calm are: not the end of life’s noise, but a way of hearing it without flinching.
